q-114952.name: Question 1
q-114952.worked_solution:
First, we let

$$
I=\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{2}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{4x}\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{2}⁡x(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4})(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{4}-2\int \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{4}-2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $I,$ remembering to add a constant of integration $C$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{4}-2I \\ 3I & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{4} \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡x}{12}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Calculate ∫ln2⁡x4xdx using integration by parts.

a
 ln3⁡x4+C
b
 ln3⁡x12+C
c
 ln3⁡x6+C
d
 ln⁡x12+C
e
 −ln⁡x3+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we let I=∫ln2⁡x4xdx.

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that u=ln2⁡x⇒dudx=2ln⁡xx,dvdx=14x⇒v=∫14xdx=ln⁡x4.

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

I=∫ln2⁡x4xdx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=ln2⁡x(ln⁡x4)−∫(ln⁡x4)(2ln⁡xx)dx=ln3⁡x4−2∫ln2⁡x4xdx=ln3⁡x4−2I.

Finally, we solve for I, remembering to add a constant of integration C at the very end: I=ln3⁡x4−2I3I=ln3⁡x4I=ln3⁡x12+C

q-114951.name: Question 2
q-114951.worked_solution:
First, we let

$$
I=\int \frac{{ln}^{8}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{8}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{8{ln}^{7}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{8}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{8}⁡x(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)(\frac{8{ln}^{7}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{9}⁡x-8\int \frac{{ln}^{8}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{9}⁡x-8I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $I,$ remembering to add a constant of integration $C$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={ln}^{9}⁡x-8I \\ 9I & ={ln}^{9}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{9}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-348879.name: Question 3
q-348879.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int \frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{6x}\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{4}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{4{ln}^{3}⁡x}{x}, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{6x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{6x}\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{6x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{4}⁡x)(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{6})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{6})(\frac{4{ln}^{3}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{6}-4\int \frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{6x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{6}-4I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $I.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{6}-4I \\ 5I & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{6} \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{5}⁡x}{30}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{3}}\frac{{ln}^{4}⁡x}{6x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{30}({ln}^{5}⁡x)\,{|}_{1}^{{e}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{30}({ln}^{5}⁡({e}^{3})-{ln}^{5}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{30}((3\operatorname{ln}⁡e)^{5}-{0}^{5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{30}({3}^{5}-0) \\  & =\frac{81}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

q-49976.name: Question 5
q-49976.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int \frac{{ln}^{3}⁡z}{z}\,\text{d}z.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{3}⁡z\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}=\frac{3{ln}^{2}⁡z}{z}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}z}=\frac{1}{z}\, & ⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{z}\,\text{d}z=\operatorname{ln}⁡z.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{3}⁡z}{z}\,\text{d}z \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}z}\,\text{d}z \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={ln}^{3}⁡z(\operatorname{ln}⁡z)-\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡z)(\frac{3{ln}^{2}⁡z}{z})\,\text{d}z \\  & ={ln}^{4}⁡z-3\int \frac{{ln}^{3}⁡z}{z}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={ln}^{4}⁡z-3I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $I.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={ln}^{4}⁡z-3I \\ 4I & ={ln}^{4}⁡z \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{4}⁡z}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{{ln}^{3}⁡z}{z}\,\text{d}z & =\frac{1}{4}({ln}^{4}⁡z){|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}({ln}^{4}⁡(e)-{ln}^{4}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

q-3402.name: Question 6
q-3402.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)({e}^{x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)({e}^{x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\int {e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-J \\ I & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-(-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+I) \\ I & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-I \\ 2I & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-114950.name: Question 7
q-114950.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3{e}^{-3x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-3x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(-3{e}^{-3x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\int {e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3{e}^{-3x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-3x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-3{e}^{-3x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-3\int {e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-3I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3J \\ I & ={e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3(-{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-3I) \\ I & ={e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-9I \\ 10I & ={e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{10}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-15409.name: Question 8
q-15409.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2J \\ I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2({e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2I) \\ I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4I \\ 5I & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{5}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-12924.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}J \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}(\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}I) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{9}-\frac{1}{9}I \\ \frac{10}{9}I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{10}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-3397.name: Question 10
q-3397.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})(2{e}^{2x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})(2{e}^{2x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}J \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}(\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}I) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{9}-\frac{4}{9}I \\ \frac{13}{9}I & =\frac{2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-3{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{2x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{13}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-83014.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}J \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}(\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{1}{3}I) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{9}-\frac{1}{9}I \\ \frac{10}{9}I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =(-\frac{{e}^{-x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{10}){|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-\pi /3}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3})+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}))}{10}+\frac{{e}^{-0}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot 0)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot 0))}{10} \\  & =\frac{3{e}^{-\pi /3}}{10}+\frac{3}{10} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}({e}^{-\pi /3}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}J \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}I) \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4}-\frac{1}{4}I \\ \frac{5}{4}I & =\frac{2{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4} \\ I & =\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-\pi /2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})))-(\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-0}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(0))-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(0)))) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi /2}}{5}+\frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi /2}+1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

q-115003.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{e}^{-2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-2x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-2{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2\int {e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2J \\ I & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2(-{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2I) \\ I & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4I \\ 5I & ={e}^{-2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{-2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{-2\pi /2}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})))-(\frac{{e}^{-2(0)}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡0-2\operatorname{cos}⁡0)) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi }}{5}+\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}({e}^{-\pi }+2)\end{aligned}
$$

q-362669.problem:
Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{10}($
{{field-1}} $)$
q-362669.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by  $I=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =({e}^{-x})(\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))-\int (\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))(-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+\frac{1}{3}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =({e}^{-x})(-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))-\int (-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))(-{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-\frac{1}{3}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+\frac{1}{3}J \\ I & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+\frac{1}{3}(-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-\frac{1}{3}I) \\ I & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-\frac{1}{9}I \\ 10I & ={e}^{-x}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)) \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}}{10}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{{e}^{-x}}{10}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{-\pi }}{10}(0-(-1)))-(\frac{1}{10}(0-1)) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi }}{10}+\frac{1}{10} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}({e}^{-\pi }+1).\end{aligned}
$$

q-115005.name: Question 15
q-115005.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+J \\ I & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-I) \\ I & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-I \\ 2I & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)){|}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{-\pi }}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ))-(\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi ))) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi }}{2}-\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{2} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi }-{e}^{\pi }}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Let's denote the indefinite integral by I=∫e−xcos⁡xdx.

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that u=e−x⇒dudx=−e−x,dvdx=cos⁡x⇒v=∫cos⁡xdx=sin⁡x.

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get I=∫e−xcos⁡xdx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=e−x(sin⁡x)−∫(sin⁡x)(−e−x)dx=e−xsin⁡x+∫e−xsin⁡xdx=e−xsin⁡x+J.

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate J=∫e−xsin⁡xdx.

To do this, let's suppose that u=e−x⇒dudx=−e−x,dvdx=sin⁡x⇒v=∫sin⁡xdx=−cos⁡x.

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get J=∫e−xsin⁡xdx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=e−x(−cos⁡x)−∫(−cos⁡x)(−e−x)dx=−e−xcos⁡x−∫e−xcos⁡xdx=−e−xcos⁡x−I.

So, substituting this into our equation for I, we can subsequently solve for I: I=e−xsin⁡x+JI=e−xsin⁡x+(−e−xcos⁡x−I)I=e−xsin⁡x−e−xcos⁡x−I2I=e−xsin⁡x−e−xcos⁡xI=e−x2(sin⁡x−cos⁡x)

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows: ∫−ππe−xcos⁡xdx=(e−x2(sin⁡x−cos⁡x))|−ππ=(e−π2(sin⁡π−cos⁡π))−(eπ2(sin⁡(−π)−cos⁡(−π)))=e−π2−eπ2=e−π−eπ2
